💡 Nearly half of the top cryptocurrencies are now outperforming Bitcoin

Over the past three months, 47% of the top 50 coins by market cap have delivered better returns than BTC. Capital is clearly flowing into altcoins — but it's doing so very selectively. 🧐

The last time a majority of altcoins outperformed Bitcoin was in September 2025, just before the market's final rally and local top.

Does this mean altseason has started? Not exactly. 

The current market looks very different:

🔹Innovative projects are attracting capital and outperforming.
🔹Older and weaker altcoins continue making new lows.
🔹Liquidity is concentrated in a small group of winners.

The biggest mistake right now may be buying everything and hoping for a broad altseason.

So far, this is a market of selective winners, not a rising tide lifting all boats. Historically, a true altseason begins only when the majority of altcoins start outperforming Bitcoin — and we're not there yet. 👀

📌 Bonding Curves: How Token Prices Move With Every Buy and Sell

Main Points
⏺ Bonding curves define a token’s price as a math function of supply
⏺ Every buy pushes the price up along the curve; every sell pushes it down
⏺ This post explains why bonding curves are popular for launches and micro-caps

1️⃣ Core Concept — instead of an order book, a smart contract sets the price based on how many tokens are already minted or held.
2️⃣ Automatic Pricing — early buyers get cheaper tokens; as demand increases, the curve raises the price automatically.
3️⃣ Liquidity Built-In — the contract always stands ready to buy back tokens along the same curve, so there’s no traditional LP needed.
4️⃣ Design Choices — steeper curves pump price faster but are more volatile; flatter curves are smoother but less “explosive.”
5️⃣ Risks — thin real liquidity, manipulation, and the fact that math-driven pricing doesn’t guarantee real fundamental value.

Final Thoughts

Bonding curves turn token price into a formula instead of a market guess — transparent, but still only as meaningful as the demand behind it.

Cheap Oil, Expensive “Peace”

Trump’s team just rewired the Iran war into a 60‑day oil subsidy. Washington issues a temporary license: Iran can legally sell crude on the international market, at full prices, after years of dumping under‑the‑table barrels at sanctions discounts. In return, there is no concrete nuclear deal — just talk, committees, and a PR fight over who promised what on inspections.

JD Vance calls the first Swiss round “very very good,” claims Tehran agreed to let UN inspectors back into nuclear sites, and Trump blasts online that Iran will accept “Major Weapons Inspections” and “nuclear honesty” for years ahead. 

Iranian officials answer flatly: no new commitments, no nuclear clauses in these talks, any IAEA access will be under existing procedures — meaning the limited, heavily managed regime that survived after Trump killed the 2015 deal and before strikes pushed inspectors out. One side sells a breakthrough; the other sells continuity.

Meanwhile, the real leverage sits in Hormuz and Lebanon. Iran is already ramping up exports now that the US naval blockade is lifted, but openly warns that if Israel keeps hitting Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, it will keep using the strait as a choke point. 

Vance talks about mechanisms to “keep Hormuz open” and de‑confliction cells for Lebanon, yet refuses to say clearly whether Washington is pushing Israel to pull troops from the south. The message to Tehran: you get oil and some cash as long as you don’t blow up the shipping lanes; the message from Tehran: we decide when the lanes stay open.

Trump tries to reassure critics by saying Iran is “supposed to” use the new money to buy food, not weapons. Vance even floats that Tehran will spend unfrozen funds on American soy, wheat and corn. 

But the memorandum explicitly lets Iran’s central bank choose where the cash goes, and there’s no sign in Iranian messaging that they’ve agreed to become a captive customer for Midwestern agribusiness. Washington gets talking points; Tehran gets options.

So the “oil waiver” is not a technicality. It’s the core of the trade: immediate economic lifeline for Iran, short‑term price relief for Trump’s voters, and a big IOU on everything the war was sold on — nukes, missiles, proxies, and “neither a dollar nor a drop” for Tehran’s military. 

The battlefield pauses, the tankers move, and both sides declare progress, while the hard questions are shoved into committees that may never outlive this 60‑day grace period.
